<reason>Both sides built credible cases, but B's late-stage dialectics were cleaner and A accumulated execution costs. A's opening chokepoint framing and essential-facility analogy (the phone company) were the debate's most memorable moves, and the "solely" textual reading was sharp. However, A was clipped for word limits in three turns (opening, both rebuttals), left B's product/seller operational criterion (B4.2) unrebutted after claiming "no distinction exists," never answered the boutique-overreach point that the motion contains no dominance exception (B3.1, B4.4-B4.5), and framed B's test in closing as exclusion because partners "might" object after B had explicitly rejected speculative losses — a mischaracterization B immediately corrected. B answered A's pressure questions with concrete enforceable duties (notice, review, substantiation, less restrictive measures), delivered the requested operational criterion, and consistently hammered A's absolutist "absorb every cost except misconduct" concession. B's closing crystallized the real choice accurately. A's rhetorical edge kept it competitive, but B made the debate easier to decide and held the stronger unrebutted routes.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B4.1-B4.3: B directly answered both pressure questions with a substantive framework (evidentiary threshold, less restrictive measures, independent review) and the product-vs-seller distinction that defeated A's claim that no operational criterion separated reputational exclusion from racial discrimination; A never squarely rebutted it, and A's closing mischaracterization of B's test handed B the final exchange.</best_rebuttal>
